entry.evidence: the previous dating and sequence stratigraphic interpretations of the Tierwis Formation often did not come to an agreement

sequences.source_document: Publisher XML full text (jats_text), checked against published PDF

steps.action: States the problem: earlier dating and sequence-stratigraphic interpretations of the Tierwis Formation disagree because biomarkers are unevenly distributed, which leaves platform onset and drowning-surface correlations doubtful.
steps.quote: the previous dating and sequence stratigraphic interpretations of the Tierwis Formation often did not come to an agreement

steps.action: Takes from earlier work the postulated link between platform drowning phases, palaeoceanographic change and OAE black shales, and uses it as the framework for correlation.
steps.quote: Föllmi et al. (50) and Weissert et al. (115) postulated possible links between drowning phases, palaeoceanographic and/or paleoenvironmental change affecting carbonate factories.

steps.action: Cites the published hypothesis of Bodin et al. (2006a) that the Chopf Bed corresponds to the Tierwis–Schrattenkalk transition in the proximal Säntis sections.
steps.quote: Bodin et al. (10) presumed that the Chopf Bed stratigraphically corresponds to the transition between the Tierwis and the Schrattenkalk formations

steps.action: Sets the aim: a new high-resolution biostratigraphic and sedimentological model of the Tierwis Formation, discussed against environmental change and OAEs.
steps.quote: The present study presents a new high-resolution biostratigraphical and sedimentological model of the Tierwis Formation in the Alpstein massif.

steps.action: Carries out field logging and collects more than 200 ammonites from the Tierwis, Langtal, Altmann and Litten-Chreialp outcrops, extended to Alp Wis and Frümsner Alp, and dates them on the Kilian Group Tethyan zonation.
steps.quote: We carried out a sedimentological and palaeontological field study based on a large number of ammonite (> 200 specimens)

steps.action: Uses phosphorus and C–O stable isotope data measured by Bonvallet (2015, 2019) on 83 Tierwis samples and labels the isotope segments after Wissler, splitting B1 and adding Hy and Hz.
steps.quote: Geochemical measurements used here were performed by Bonvallet (14) and Bonvallet et al. (15).

steps.action: Refines the frameworks: adds a new sequence boundary SB B3' to Arnaud's (2005) scheme, and replaces the glauconite-based Altmann/Drusberg boundary with the upper phosphatic conglomerate as marker bed (§3 ¶4).
steps.quote: an additional key surface is recognized at the boundary between the T. vandenheckii and the G. sartousiana zones

steps.action: Dates the Tierwis section beds by ammonite biostratigraphy (B. catulloi Subzone, T. hugii Zone, K. nicklesi/N. pulchella zones, K. compressissima–M. moutonianum, T. vandenheckii), using new finds and a re-examination of older material.
steps.quote: The newly collected material as well as our reinvestigation of previously reported fossils allow the stratigraphic assignment to the B. catulloi Subzone.

steps.action: Reports Bonvallet's phosphorus peaks P1–P5 in the condensed beds and the δ13C fluctuations at Tierwis, and divides the δ13C curve into seven segments (Fig. 5).
steps.quote: The phosphorus content (P, orange line in Fig. 5) of the Tierwis Formation was measured by Bonvallet (14).

steps.action: Logs the Altmann section on its more complete, fault-free SW side and dates the polyzonal upper phosphatic conglomerate there from N. pulchella Zone to G. alpinum Subzone using a large ammonite fauna.
steps.quote: This diverse faunal association indicates the Nicklesia pulchella Zone to the Gassendiceras alpinum Subzone.

steps.action: Observes at Litten-Chreialp two superimposed generations of erosional depressions and channels filled by Altmann Member subunits, and dates the conglomerate there from earliest Barremian to G. alpinum Subzone.
steps.quote: The top of the Helvetischer Kieselkalk Formation is deeply eroded, showing two superimposed erosional surfaces

steps.action: Chooses the Zeheloch section because there the whole Drusberg Member is exposed (scree covers parts of it at Litten-Chreialp), and logs the D12 firmground and the glauconitic bed above it.
steps.quote: we studied the Zeheloch section where the entire member is exposed

steps.action: Prospects the south-eastern range and finds at Frümsner Alp and Alp Wis an ammonite-bearing phosphatic conglomerate above a glauconitic firmground, dated H. fallax to G. sartousiana subzones.
steps.quote: exposes the same phosphatic conglomerate with belemnite rostra and the ammonites

steps.action: Compares the dating and depositional geometry of the Tierwis paratype and Altmann type sections, defines subunits A1–A3, and concludes that the two sections cover different intervals.
steps.quote: reveals that the Altmann Member of the Tierwis paratype section and the Altmann type section do not cover the same stratigraphic interval

steps.action: Proposes two causes for the channelization and thickness changes, syntectonic tilted blocks and bottom-current winnowing, and retains both without deciding between them.
steps.quote: Two processes seem to be involved in such channelization, a syntectonic activity and the bottom-sea winnowing, acting independently or simultaneously.

steps.action: Argues that the classical glauconite-based boundary cannot be mapped and tentatively proposes the upper phosphatic conglomerate as the boundary between the Altmann and Drusberg members.
steps.quote: We tentatively suggest this boundary between the Altmann and Drusberg members

steps.action: Infers from the ammonite ranges in the conglomerate at three sections that the upper phosphatic conglomerate is diachronic and spans more time towards the open sea (SE).
steps.quote: Thus, the upper phosphatic conglomerate is diachronic, containing an increasing period of time in south-eastward direction

steps.action: Divides the Drusberg Member into subunits D1 and D2, separated by limestone S1 or by the Chopf Bed, and dates them by ammonites (D2 = G. sartousiana Subzone; transect in Fig. 16, p. 22).
steps.quote: The subunit D2 is dated by ammonites to the G. sartousiana Subzone.

steps.action: Takes from Föllmi et al. (2006) the expected signature of a drowning phase: sea-level rise, glauconite and phosphate authigenesis, and a subsequent positive δ13C excursion.
steps.quote: the authors stated that each drowning phase was quickly followed by a major positive carbon-isotope excursion

steps.action: Matches the marker beds against the expected signature (P excursions, δ13C fluctuations, condensation, ammonite bio-events), interprets them as drowning phases, and recognizes six event beds of regional significance.
steps.quote: We recognized six lithologically, chemically and biologically exceptional event beds of regional significance

steps.action: Supports the P. ohmi dating of surface D2, and hence the SB H6 attribution of D1, with ammonites from the same bed in other sections (Oberlänggli, Schwendi).
steps.quote: This dating is reinforced by additional ammonites originating from this bed from other sections

steps.action: Checks the ammonite-based link of the first glauconitic level (MFS H6) to the Faraoni event against an independent proxy, the negative δ13C peak C1.
steps.quote: The attribution of our glauconitic level to the Faraoni episode is herein corroborated by δ13C values

steps.action: Correlates the second glauconitic level (SB/MFS H7, P2, δ13C peak C2) with the Clos de Barral condensed interval and with Tethyan and Lower Saxony black shales (Fig. 17, p. 25), and names a tentative 'Hugii' event.
steps.quote: which suggest to consider this level as a regional event, tentatively called “Hugii” event

steps.action: Correlates the marly bioturbated level in the upper Altmann Member (MFS B1, P3, δ13C peak C3) with the Angles sequence scheme and names a tentative 'Pulchella' event.
steps.quote: pointing to a probable additional regional event, tentatively called “Pulchella event”

steps.action: Infers how long the hiatus lasted at each section from the time span recorded in the polyzonal upper phosphatic conglomerate (whole of B1' at Tierwis, up to B3 at Altmann and Litten-Chreialp).
steps.quote: The time span comprised in the phosphatic conglomerate is herein considered as indicative of the duration of this hiatus

steps.action: Keeps an ammonite calibration of the Mid-Barremian Event in the Helvetic record.
steps.quote: The MBE is herein calibrated by ammonites from the Moutoniceras moutonianum Zone to the Toxancyloceras vandenheckii Zone pro parte.

steps.action: Compares the ammonite ages of the SE-range conglomerate with those of the Chopf Bed at its type locality, finds them contemporaneous, attributes the bed to the Chopf Bed and D12 to SB B3'.
steps.quote: These two beds are therefore contemporaneous, which allowed us to attribute our phosphatic conglomerate to the Chopf Bed.

steps.action: Rejects the published assumption that the Chopf Bed marks the Drusberg–Schrattenkalk transition in the proximal Säntis sections.
steps.quote: Contrary to the assumptions of Bodin et al. (11) and Bonvallet et al. (15), the Chopf Bed does not correspond to the transition

steps.action: Keeps the conclusion that the dated marker beds record two major drowning phases (Faraoni, MBE) and four minor key beds, tentatively correlated with other basins.
steps.quote: point to a total of two major drowning phases and associated environmental change (Faraoni and MBE events) as well as four minor key-beds

steps.action: Leaves open hypotheses for future tests: the boundary applies outside the Alpstein, and the landward equivalent of the Chopf Bed lies within the Schrattenkalk Formation.
steps.quote: An upcoming detailed study of the Schrattenkalk Formation in the Alpstein massif will bring new insights allowing to test this hypothesis.

No; ages and drowning phases are inferred from ammonites, geometry and geochemical traces
Re-date the formation and its key surfaces, and correlate them with environmental events

Partly; the ammonite age of the Chopf Bed separates its position from the Schrattenkalk transition
Conditions found in outcrops along a NW–SE transect; the Zeheloch section chosen for exposure

tree.answer: The same marker beds recur in several sections and in other basins
Limited: δ13C corroboration and ammonites from other sections; correlations stay tentative
Kept as best explanation; one published assumption rejected

end.claim: New ammonite dating of the Tierwis Formation's key beds and surfaces reveals a dense succession of latest Hauterivian to late Barremian drowning phases, including two major ones linked to the Faraoni event and the onset of the Mid-Barremian Event.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the ammonite dating of key beds from newly collected fauna across the sections there would be no revised calibration of the drowning phases, member boundaries or Chopf Bed attribution.

gates.evidence: Collection was a broad field and palaeontological survey, and sections were chosen for exposure and completeness (§4.3 ¶1, §4.5 ¶1), not to test a hypothesis. The Chopf Bed attribution could have failed if the ammonite ages had differed (§5.2.6 ¶2), and the Faraoni link was checked against δ13C (§5.2.2 ¶1). Most correlations are called tentative (§6 ¶3). Nothing was fixed before the data were seen.

novelty_claims.quote: which we recognised for the first time in the Alsptein massif
We found Emericiceras koechlini (Astier, 1851) and E. emerici (Léveillé, 1837) in this level, from which no ammonites were reported previously.
Newly found marker beds such as firmgrounds and hardgrounds, glauconitic beds [...]

limits:
Outcome conflict: the headline claim is kept as best explanation, but the paper also establishes a contradiction. It rejects the published assumption (Bodin et al. 2006; Bonvallet et al. 2019) that the Chopf Bed marks the Drusberg–Schrattenkalk transition (§5.2.6 ¶2, §6 ¶4). Codebook section 7 would code that contradiction as outcome contradicted; it is recorded here as a sub-claim (contradicted, confirmed by ammonite ages).

Other sub-claims and their statuses:
- Type and paratype sections cover different intervals: best_explanation.
- The upper phosphatic conglomerate is diachronic: estimate_with_resolution, with no uncertainty stated.
- Ammonite calibration of the MBE: estimate_with_resolution.
- The new member boundary and the Hugii, Pulchella and Sartousiana events: tentative, best_explanation at most.

Data and checks:
- All geochemistry comes from earlier work (Bonvallet 2015, 2019) and from the Tierwis section only, so the δ13C and P corroborations do not extend to the other sections.
- The diagenesis check (δ13C–δ18O correlation, R2 = 0.11) is cited from Bonvallet. It is listed in v_checks as not performed here and is not coded as a V step.
- Inference: the Schwendi ammonites in step 21 seem to be the authors' own, since they are uncited, but the paper does not say so.
- The ammonite taxonomy is deferred to a separate paper (§3 ¶1), so the specimen identifications behind the dating cannot be checked here.
- No quantitative uncertainty is given for the correlations, and no alternative biozonation scheme is considered.

The acknowledgements name reviewers, but no review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded.

disagreements.target: Bodin et al. (2006b) and Bonvallet et al. (2019), Chopf Bed as the Drusberg–Schrattenkalk transition in proximal Säntis sections
disagreements.support: Ammonites from the SE-range conglomerate match the age of the Chopf Bed at its type locality, and the bed is traced landward into a discontinuity within the Schrattenkalk Formation.
disagreements.quote: Contrary to the assumptions of Bodin et al. (11) and Bonvallet et al. (15), the Chopf Bed does not correspond to the transition

disagreements.target: Classical Altmann/Drusberg boundary at the disappearance of glauconite (Briegel, Fichter, Funk, Heim)
disagreements.support: The boundary varies between authors and sections, ignores the main facies change, and is not mappable; the upper phosphatic conglomerate is proposed instead.
disagreements.quote: Such a boundary is not mappable since it does not correspond to the main lithological change

disagreements.target: Treatment of the Altmann type section and Tierwis paratype section (Funk 1969) as equivalent
disagreements.support: New ammonite dating and channel geometries show that the paratype covers only the lower third of the type section.
disagreements.quote: the Tierwis paratype section represents only the lower third of the Altmann type [...]

disagreements.target: Funk (1969) attribution of the basal echinodermic limestone to the Kieselkalk Formation
disagreements.support: The unit is placed at the base of the Altmann Member, as subunit A1, on lithological and biostratigraphic grounds.
disagreements.quote: which was first attributed to the Kieselkalk Formation by Funk (41)

disagreements.target: Previous dating of drowning phases and of the Tierwis Formation developed over recent decades
disagreements.support: The new ammonite calibration revises the ages of key surfaces and the sequence-stratigraphic interpretation.
disagreements.quote: Our revised calibration substantially modifies the dating of the drowning phases and other key surfaces

alternatives_considered.chosen: Upper phosphatic conglomerate as top of the Altmann Member
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Boundary based on presence of glauconite and/or importance of marly interbeds
alternatives_considered.reason: Better adapted to field work and mapping; the classical definition ignores the main facies boundary

alternatives_considered.chosen: Wissler carbon-isotope segment nomenclature, with B1 split into B1a/B1b and provisional Hy/Hz
alternatives_considered.alternatives: A formal nomenclature for the uppermost Hauterivian intervals (not yet available)
alternatives_considered.reason: While waiting for a formal nomenclature

alternatives_considered.chosen: SW side of Altmannsattel for the Altmann log
alternatives_considered.alternatives: NE side chosen by Funk (1969) as type section; Altmannsattel ridge
alternatives_considered.reason: More complete; the ridge is affected by a fault

alternatives_considered.chosen: Zeheloch section for the Drusberg Member
alternatives_considered.reason: Parts of the Drusberg Member are covered by scree at Litten-Chreialp

alternatives_considered.chosen: Syntectonic activity and bottom-current winnowing both retained
